subject: biology

items.q: What is a pathogen?
items.correct: A microorganism that causes infectious disease
items.misconception: A bacterium that causes an infectious disease
items.why: Students meet bacteria first and hear 'germ' and 'bacteria' used as if they mean the same thing in everyday talk. Bacteria are also the group most often drawn in textbooks, so the word pathogen gets attached to that one picture instead of to the whole group of disease-causing microorganisms. Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease. Pathogens may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi. Measles is caused by a virus, salmonella food poisoning by bacteria, malaria by protists and rose black spot by a fungus.
items.random_wrong: A poison that damages tissues and makes us ill

items.q: Purple and black spots have appeared on the leaves of a rose bush in a garden. How is this disease most likely to reach the other rose bushes in the garden?
items.correct: By water or wind in the environment
items.misconception: By insects moving between the plants
items.why: Students know that mosquitos spread malaria and generalise that a plant disease must also need a living carrier. Because plants do not move or touch, an insect feels like the only way the pathogen could cross the gap. Rose black spot is a fungal disease that is spread in the environment by water or wind. It can be treated by using fungicides and/or removing and destroying the affected leaves.
items.random_wrong: By direct contact between the leaves

items.q: What kind of pathogen causes malaria?
items.correct: A protist spread to humans by mosquitos
items.misconception: A bacterium spread to humans by mosquitos
items.why: Students meet bacteria first and hear 'germ' and 'bacteria' used as if they mean the same thing in everyday talk. Bacteria are also the group most often drawn in textbooks, so the word pathogen gets attached to that one picture instead of to the whole group of disease-causing microorganisms. Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease. Pathogens may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi. Measles is caused by a virus, salmonella food poisoning by bacteria, malaria by protists and rose black spot by a fungus.
items.random_wrong: A mosquito that bites and infects humans

items.q: A health agency wants to reduce the number of malaria cases in a region. Which approach should it use?
items.correct: Stopping mosquitos breeding and using nets
items.misconception: Treating infected people with antibiotics
items.why: The word antibiotic sounds like a general anti-life or anti-germ medicine. Patients often recover after taking antibiotics prescribed for something else, and viral illnesses get better on their own, so the medicine appears to have worked. Antibiotics, such as penicillin, are medicines that help to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body. Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens. It is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the body's tissues.

items.q: How is the spread of salmonella food poisoning controlled in the UK?
items.correct: Poultry are vaccinated against salmonella
items.misconception: People are vaccinated against salmonella
items.why: Every other vaccination example students meet is a human one, so they assume the pattern continues. They also miss that salmonella reaches people through food, which means the sensible place to break the chain is in the animals that the food comes from. Salmonella food poisoning is spread by bacteria ingested in food, or on food prepared in unhygienic conditions. In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.
items.random_wrong: Poultry are treated with strong antibiotics

items.q: Which of these is a non-specific defence system of the human body?
items.correct: The stomach produces acid that kills pathogens
items.misconception: The nose produces antibodies to attack pathogens
items.why: Students meet the barriers and the immune response in the same lesson and merge them into a single defence story. Antibody is the strongest word in that story, so it gets attached to every part of it. Non-specific defence systems of the human body include the skin, nose, trachea and bronchi, and stomach. They act against pathogens in general. Antibody production, along with phagocytosis and antitoxin production, is how white blood cells help to defend against pathogens once they are inside.
items.random_wrong: Cilia in the trachea destroy trapped pathogens

items.q: Bacteria in the blood are releasing toxins. Which action of the white blood cells deals with those toxins?
items.correct: The production of antitoxins
items.misconception: The production of antibodies
items.why: Antibody is the more familiar word and gets used as a general label for anything the immune system makes. The words antibody, antitoxin and antigen also look and sound alike, so students pick the one they have heard most. White blood cells help to defend against pathogens by: phagocytosis; antibody production; antitoxin production. Antibodies act against the pathogen itself, while antitoxins counteract the toxins that bacteria produce.

items.q: A pathogen gets past the body's non-specific defences and enters the body for the first time. What does the immune system do?
items.correct: It tries to destroy the invading pathogen
items.misconception: It produces toxins to kill the pathogen
items.why: Toxin is the first mechanism students learn for feeling ill, so it becomes the explanation for every infection. Students also hear 'toxic' used loosely for anything harmful, which makes it sound like the general reason a pathogen causes harm. Bacteria may produce poisons (toxins) that damage tissues and make us feel ill. Viruses cause harm in a different way: they live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage.
items.random_wrong: It develops resistance to the pathogen

items.q: What is introduced into the body during a vaccination?
items.correct: Dead or inactive forms of a pathogen
items.misconception: Ready-made antibodies from donors
items.why: Students know a vaccine leaves you with antibodies and reason backwards that the antibodies must have been in the syringe. The idea that you have to be given the pathogen in order to be protected from it feels contradictory, so the simpler story wins. Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies. The antibodies are made by the body, not supplied by the vaccine.
items.random_wrong: Live and active forms of a pathogen

items.q: A large proportion of the population in a town is vaccinated against measles. What is the effect on the people in that town who are not vaccinated?
items.correct: They are less likely to catch measles
items.misconception: They are equally likely to catch measles
items.why: Vaccination is taught as something that happens to an individual body, so students reason only about that body. The population level effect needs a picture of how a pathogen travels from person to person, which is a separate idea students have not linked in. Students should be able to explain how vaccination will prevent illness in an individual, and how the spread of pathogens can be reduced by immunising a large proportion of the population. With most people immune, the pathogen has far fewer people to infect and pass through, so people who are not vaccinated are less likely to meet it.
items.random_wrong: They are made immune to measles as well

items.q: A patient has a viral infection and a painful sore throat. Which treatment is appropriate, and why?
items.correct: Painkillers, which treat the symptoms
items.misconception: Antibiotics, which kill the pathogen
items.why: The word antibiotic sounds like a general anti-life or anti-germ medicine. Patients often recover after taking antibiotics prescribed for something else, and viral illnesses get better on their own, so the medicine appears to have worked. Antibiotics, such as penicillin, are medicines that help to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body. Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens. It is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the body's tissues.

items.q: The use of antibiotics greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases, but some bacterial infections are now much harder to treat. Why?
items.correct: Resistant strains of bacteria have emerged
items.misconception: Patients have grown resistant to antibiotics
items.why: Everyday phrases such as 'I have become resistant to it' put the patient at the centre of the sentence. Students also think of resistance as something a body builds up, like a tolerance, rather than as a property of a population of bacteria. The use of antibiotics has greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases. However, the emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern. It is the strain of bacteria that is resistant to the antibiotic.
items.random_wrong: Antibiotics have started to kill viruses too

items.q: Why is it difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses?
items.correct: Viruses live in cells, so tissues are damaged
items.misconception: Viruses reproduce outside the body's cells
items.why: Both bacteria and viruses are described as reproducing rapidly inside the body, and students merge the two statements into one. The phrase 'inside the body' is read as 'inside the cells', so the special feature of viruses is applied to bacteria as well. Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage. Bacteria and viruses may both reproduce rapidly inside the body, but bacteria make us feel ill mainly because they may produce poisons (toxins) that damage tissues.
items.random_wrong: Viruses make toxins that destroy the drugs

items.q: A pharmaceutical company has synthesised a possible new drug. Which describes the preclinical testing of that drug?
items.correct: Testing on cells, tissues and live animals
items.misconception: Testing on healthy volunteers, patients
items.why: The word clinical is heard inside preclinical, so the two stages blur together. Students also remember that healthy volunteers come early in the process and attach 'early' to the earliest stage they can name. Preclinical testing is done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals. Clinical trials come afterwards and use healthy volunteers and patients.
items.random_wrong: Testing on patients at the optimum dose

items.q: What happens in a double blind trial?
items.correct: Some patients are given a placebo
items.misconception: Some patients get a smaller dose
items.why: Students learn in the same breath that trials start with very low doses and that some patients get a placebo, and they fuse the two facts. Low dose and no drug both sound like 'less', so the distinction is lost. Clinical trials use healthy volunteers and patients. Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the clinical trial, and further trials find the optimum dose. In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo, which is not the drug being tested.
items.random_wrong: Healthy volunteers are in the trial

items.q: Which drug is correctly matched with the source it originally came from?
items.correct: Digitalis is extracted from foxgloves
items.misconception: Aspirin is extracted from foxgloves
items.why: Two drugs and two plants are learned as one list, and there is no link between the names to hold the pairs together. Under pressure students recall that both pairs exist but not which goes with which. Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms. The heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves. The painkiller aspirin originates from willow.

items.q: Why must new medical drugs be tested and trialled before they are used?
items.correct: To check they are safe and effective
items.misconception: To check they kill bacterial pathogens
items.why: The word antibiotic sounds like a general anti-life or anti-germ medicine. Patients often recover after taking antibiotics prescribed for something else, and viral illnesses get better on their own, so the medicine appears to have worked. Antibiotics, such as penicillin, are medicines that help to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body. Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens. It is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging the body's tissues.
items.random_wrong: To check they remove painful symptoms

items.q: How are most new drugs produced today?
items.correct: Synthesised by pharmaceutical chemists
items.misconception: Extracted from plants and microorganisms
items.why: Digitalis and aspirin are both plant drugs and are usually listed first, so students generalise the pattern to penicillin. The historical examples are memorable and get carried forward as a description of how drugs are made now. Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms; penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould, which is a microorganism and not a plant. Most new drugs are synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry, although the starting point may still be a chemical extracted from a plant.
items.random_wrong: Extracted from the willow and foxgloves

items.q: Do you have to touch an infected person or plant to catch a disease from them?
items.correct: Pathogens can be spread by direct contact, by water or by air, so contact between hosts is not needed for many diseases.
items.misconception: A pathogen can only pass from one host to another if the two make direct contact, so a disease cannot spread across a gap.
items.why: Direct contact is the route students can picture most easily and it is listed first. Water and air are invisible carriers, so students do not treat them as real routes and look for a moment of touching instead. Pathogens may infect plants or animals and can be spread by direct contact, by water or by air. The measles virus is spread by inhalation of droplets from sneezes and coughs, and rose black spot is spread in the environment by water or wind.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does someone who is infected with HIV have AIDS?
items.correct: HIV initially causes a flu-like illness, and late stage HIV infection, or AIDS, occurs only when the immune system becomes so badly damaged it can no longer deal with other infections or cancers.
items.misconception: HIV and AIDS are two words for the same thing, so a person who catches HIV has AIDS from the moment they are infected.
items.why: The two terms are used side by side in the media, often as the single phrase 'HIV/AIDS'. Students who do not meet the time course of the infection have no reason to separate the virus from the late stage condition it can lead to. HIV initially causes a flu-like illness. Unless successfully controlled with antiretroviral drugs the virus attacks the body's immune cells. Late stage HIV infection, or AIDS, occurs when the body's immune system becomes so badly damaged it can no longer deal with other infections or cancers.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is penicillin still an easy way to treat gonorrhoea?
items.correct: Gonorrhoea was easily treated with the antibiotic penicillin until many resistant strains appeared.
items.misconception: Gonorrhoea is a bacterial disease, so penicillin will still clear it up as easily as it always did.
items.why: Students learn that antibiotics such as penicillin cure bacterial disease and apply that rule without a time dimension. Resistance is taught as a general worry rather than as something that has already changed the treatment of a named disease. Gonorrhoea is caused by a bacterium and was easily treated with the antibiotic penicillin until many resistant strains appeared. The emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern, and the spread can also be controlled by the use of a barrier method of contraception such as a condom.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the mosquito the pathogen that causes malaria?
items.correct: The pathogens that cause malaria are protists. The malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito.
items.misconception: The mosquito is the pathogen, so malaria is a disease caused by the insect that bites you.
items.why: The mosquito is the only part of the story students can see, and control measures all target the mosquito, so it looks like the cause. The protist is microscopic and never appears in the everyday account of the disease. The pathogens that cause malaria are protists. The malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito, which acts as the vector. The spread of malaria is controlled by preventing the vectors, mosquitos, from breeding and by using mosquito nets to avoid being bitten.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What do the cilia in the trachea and bronchi do to pathogens?
items.correct: The trachea and bronchi produce mucus that traps pathogens, and the cilia waft that mucus away from the lungs.
items.misconception: The cilia lining the trachea and bronchi kill the pathogens they catch.
items.why: Students learn that this is a defence system and assume that every defence destroys the pathogen. The moving hairs look active, so it is easy to imagine them attacking rather than simply moving trapped mucus. The non-specific defence systems include the trachea and bronchi, which trap pathogens in mucus that cilia then waft away from the lungs. Killing pathogens with acid is what the stomach does; destroying pathogens that get into the body is the job of the immune system.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is engulfing pathogens the only thing white blood cells do?
items.correct: White blood cells help to defend against pathogens by phagocytosis, by antibody production and by antitoxin production.
items.misconception: White blood cells defend the body by eating pathogens, and that is the whole of what they do.
items.why: Phagocytosis is the one mechanism that is easy to draw and is usually shown first, so it becomes the image students keep. Antibodies and antitoxins are chemicals rather than actions, so they are harder to picture and get dropped from the answer. White blood cells help to defend against pathogens by: phagocytosis; antibody production; antitoxin production.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a vaccine give you a mild dose of the live disease?
items.correct: Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen.
items.misconception: A vaccine contains a small amount of the live, active pathogen, so it gives you a mild version of the illness that then makes you immune.
items.why: The phrase 'small quantities' is remembered but 'dead or inactive' is not, leaving the idea of a small live dose. Feeling briefly unwell after a vaccination seems to confirm that a mild version of the disease has been given. Vaccination involves introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies. If the same pathogen re-enters the body the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies, preventing infection.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Will any antibiotic clear up any bacterial infection?
items.correct: It is important that specific bacteria should be treated by specific antibiotics.
items.misconception: One antibiotic works as well as another, so any bacterial disease can be treated with whichever antibiotic is to hand.
items.why: Antibiotics are described in one sentence as medicines that kill bacteria, which sounds like a single job done by a single kind of drug. Students rarely see the range of different antibiotics, so they treat the word as naming one medicine. Antibiotics, such as penicillin, are medicines that help to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body. It is important that specific bacteria should be treated by specific antibiotics.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do painkillers cure an infection?
items.correct: Painkillers and other medicines are used to treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens.
items.misconception: A painkiller makes the illness go away, so it must be killing the pathogen that is causing it.
items.why: The word painkiller contains 'kill', and students feel better after taking one, which looks like a cure. Most illnesses that painkillers are taken for clear up by themselves, so the medicine seems to have done the work. Painkillers and other medicines are used to treat the symptoms of disease but do not kill pathogens. Antibiotics help to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What dose is given at the start of a clinical trial?
items.correct: Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the clinical trial.
items.misconception: Trials begin by giving the optimum dose, because there is no point testing an amount that is too small to work.
items.why: Students think of a trial as a test of whether the drug works and reason that a working dose is needed from the outset. The purpose of the first stage, which is checking safety rather than effect, is easy to overlook. Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the clinical trial. If the drug is found to be safe, further clinical trials are carried out to find the optimum dose for the drug.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
